Early Embryonic Development: Fertilization & Implantation

A study companion that organizes the 2026 lecture into mechanisms, timelines, contrasts, and clinical application.

FertilizationWeek 1ImplantationBilaminar DiscPregnancy Testing
Source priority: the 2026 Manuel lecture slides are the primary source. The official Week 10 learning objectives define scope. The MCG 2029 AI handout is secondary enrichment where it adds mechanisms or clinical application not spelled out on the current slides.

Learning-objective map

LO 1. Follow egg and sperm from ovulation/transport through fertilization; explain polyspermy prevention and pronuclear fusion.
LO 2. Explain cleavage, compaction, morula/blastocyst formation, and the embryoblast-versus-trophoblast split in week 1.
LO 3. Explain week 2 implantation, early trophoblast differentiation, bilaminar disc formation, and extraembryonic structures.
LO 4. Apply the sequence to early pregnancy, pregnancy testing, infertility, and assisted reproduction.

The one sequence to know

Master sequence: meiosis/gametogenesis → ovulation → sperm capacitation → fertilization in the ampulla → cleavage → morula → blastocyst → zona shedding → implantation → trophoblast splits → embryoblast splits → hCG + lacunae + bilaminar disc.
Approx. timeDevelopmental eventHigh-yield anchor
Day 1FertilizationAmpulla; zygote forms
Days 2-3Cleavage → morulaRepeated mitoses while moving through uterine tube
Days 4-5BlastocystTrophoblast outside; embryoblast inside; zona disappears
Days 5-7Early implantationBlastocyst attaches at embryonic pole
Day 8Trophoblast + embryoblast each splitCyto/syncytio + epi/hypoblast; amniotic cavity begins
Day 9Lacunar stage + primary yolk sacSyncytial vacuoles coalesce; hypoblast lines cavity
Days 11-12Implantation essentially completeBlastocyst fully embedded; surface epithelium closes defect

1. Gamete preparation: what is actually ready to fertilize?

Oocyte

  • All oogonia become primary oocytes before birth.
  • Primary oocytes remain arrested in prophase I.
  • LH signals resumption of meiosis I near ovulation.
  • The ovulated cell is a secondary oocyte arrested in metaphase II.
  • Meiosis II finishes only if fertilization occurs.

Sperm

  • Spermatogenesis begins at puberty.
  • All four meiotic products can become mature gametes.
  • Head contains nucleus + acrosome; tail provides motility.
  • Only capacitated sperm can fertilize the oocyte.
Current lecture, page 19: LH-driven completion of meiosis I produces the first polar body; the secondary oocyte enters meiosis II and arrests until fertilization.
Do not mix these up
Meiosis I separates homologous chromosomes. Meiosis II separates sister chromatids. There is no DNA replication between I and II.
2029 handout enrichment
The older companion adds two useful transport anchors: the oocyte is viable for about 24 hours after ovulation, while sperm may remain viable for several days (up to ~5 days in that handout). Treat these as enrichment; the current slides explicitly say sperm survive “several days.”

2. Fertilization: barriers, reactions, and the zygote

Core mechanism: capacitation → corona radiata → zona pellucida/acrosomal reaction → sperm-oocyte membrane fusion → block to polyspermy → oocyte completes meiosis II → male + female pronuclei → diploid zygote.

Where?

Ampulla of the uterine tube.

Acrosome

Contains enzymes that enable sperm to penetrate the zona pellucida.

Zona reaction

Changes zona properties so it becomes impermeable to additional sperm.

Current lecture, page 27: sperm crosses corona radiata, undergoes the acrosomal reaction, penetrates the zona pellucida, and triggers a zona change that blocks additional sperm.
Why the cortical reaction matters
After sperm-oocyte fusion, the oocyte changes the zona pellucida so additional sperm cannot bind and penetrate. Failure leads to polyspermy, which the lecture identifies as incompatible with human life.
2029 handout enrichment
The older handout names ZP3 as a sperm receptor and acrosin as a protease released during the acrosome reaction. It also describes an immediate membrane depolarization (“fast block”) followed by the more durable cortical/zona reaction (“slow block”). Those molecular labels are useful enrichment, but the current slides emphasize the cortical/zona reaction.
Exam trap
Acrosomal reaction helps the sperm get in. Cortical/zona reaction helps keep other sperm out.
After fusion
Sperm entry reactivates the oocyte cell cycle. The secondary oocyte completes meiosis II → female pronucleus. The sperm nucleus forms the male pronucleus. Maternal and paternal chromosomes then combine to restore the diploid chromosome number and form the zygote.

3. Week 1: zygote → morula → blastocyst

Cleavage

Repeated mitotic division of the zygote as it travels toward the uterus. Cell number rises rapidly.

Morula

About 12-32 cells; forms around day 3; remains surrounded by zona pellucida.

Blastocyst

A fluid-filled cavity develops and cells separate into two major populations.

Zona shedding

The blastocyst sheds the zona pellucida before it can attach to endometrium.

Blastocyst componentLocationPrimary fate
TrophoblastOuter thin cell layerContributes to embryonic/fetal part of placenta
Embryoblast / inner cell massCell cluster at one poleGives rise to embryo
Blastocystic cavityFluid-filled interiorEarly cavity remodeled during week 2
Current lecture, page 36: the blastocyst separates into trophoblast and embryoblast around a fluid-filled blastocystic cavity.
2029 handout enrichment
Compaction is highlighted around the 8-cell stage, when blastomeres pack tightly and increase cell-to-cell contact. The older handout also calls inner-cell-mass cells pluripotent.

4. Week 2: implantation and the bilaminar disc

Week 2 organizing rule: the trophoblast splits into two layers and the embryoblast splits into two layers. This is the cleanest way to organize the anatomy.
Parent structureLayerWhat to know
TrophoblastCytotrophoblastInner layer; distinct cells; proliferative source of trophoblast cells
SyncytiotrophoblastOuter multinucleated invasive layer; erodes endometrium; forms lacunae; produces hCG
EmbryoblastEpiblastHigher columnar cells; adjacent to amniotic cavity; embryo proper will arise from epiblast
HypoblastSmall cuboidal cells; line blastocystic cavity and contribute to primitive yolk sac
Current lecture, page 42: syncytiotrophoblast forms lacunae and produces hCG that enters maternal blood.
Implantation mechanics
The syncytiotrophoblast secretes enzymes that erode endometrium, allowing the blastocyst to burrow into the uterine lining. Nearby decidual cells accumulate glycogen and lipid, providing a nutrient-rich local environment.

Amniotic cavity

A cavity appears in the epiblast. Epiblast cells adjacent to cytotrophoblast become amnioblasts.

Primitive yolk sac

Hypoblast cells migrate to line the blastocystic cavity, creating the primary yolk sac/exocoelomic cavity.

Current lecture, page 53: by day 8 the embryoblast is organized into epiblast and hypoblast.
Current lecture, page 57: by days 11-12 the blastocyst is completely embedded and the surface epithelium largely closes the implantation defect.

5. Clinical application: use the mechanism

Pregnancy testing

hCG is produced by the syncytiotrophoblast. Once released into maternal blood it becomes the physiologic basis for early pregnancy testing.

Sperm-related infertility

Think about steps requiring sperm motility, capacitation, acrosome function, and successful penetration/fusion.

Oocyte-related infertility

Think about ovulation, meiotic maturation, oocyte quality, zona-related interactions, and successful completion of meiosis II after fertilization.

Implantation failure

Requires zona shedding, appropriate endometrium, trophoblast differentiation, and invasive syncytiotrophoblast function.

2029 handout enrichment for LO 4
The older handout explicitly connects the sequence to IVF, ICSI, and preimplantation genetic testing. ICSI conceptually bypasses the natural barriers that normally require motility, corona/zona penetration, and sperm-oocyte fusion. The older handout also reviews ectopic pregnancy and molar pregnancy; those are useful clinical extensions but are not developed in detail on the current slide deck.
